After putting up this post, my inbox, comments (and email!) have been flooded with racism and bigotry, people say that I’m lying about Albert pike and his relationship to the KKK. Well, below is an excerpt from Anton Chaitkin’s Substack post explaining exactly why this statue is so controversial: 

During the Black Lives Matter campaign in June 2020, a mob tore down and set fire to the statue of Confederate General Albert Pike that had stood for decades in Judiciary Square, Washington, D.C.

Now, President Trump has directed the National Park Service to restore the statue, with plans to reinstall it in its original place this October.

The media covered the 2020 mob event as part of a broader wave of indiscriminate attacks on historical monuments in the name of “woke” activism. But this statue carries a much deeper significance than was acknowledged at the time it was torn down—and it may become a political rallying point in the months ahead.

Albert Pike was the principal founder of the Ku Klux Klan shortly after the Civil War. The statue honoring him was dedicated in October 1901, only a month after the assassination of President William McKinley elevated Theodore (Teddy) Roosevelt to the presidency.

Teddy Roosevelt and his elite Anglophile allies had long campaigned to overturn Abraham Lincoln’s American System—the strategic orientation that defined the United States as a republic opposed to empire. They aimed to swing America into alignment with the British Empire, eroding its role as the global leader of anti-imperialist republics.

Pike himself was an elite Northerner who went South to foment rebellion against the Union. The erection of his statue in 1901—just after Roosevelt’s ascent—signaled to the transatlantic elite that America was being humiliated and brought back under imperial influence. The United States, in this vision, would serve as the “dumb giant” providing the muscle and money to pull Britain’s irons out of the fire.

Pike’s central role in creating the post–Civil War Ku Klux Klan was well known in Klan circles (see selections from the KKK’s own self-history below). Yet these facts, as well as his Confederate service—which Union veterans protested—were suppressed in the inscription on the statue’s pedestal.

The public “cover story” presented Pike merely as the head of the Southern jurisdiction of the Scottish Rite Masons, and as a “poet and philosopher.” Even this Masonic portrayal is misleading: the Scottish Rite in America was originally established by British and Tory interests during the Revolution to reinforce imperial influence among elites, in contrast to the republican orientation of Benjamin Franklin’s Masonic allies.

Thus, the issue is not one of “wokeness,” nor of being pro- or anti-Masonic.

Surely, President Trump does not intend to blindly restore a statue honoring the founder of America’s Ku Klux Klan, in the heart of a predominantly Black city that is also the nation’s capital.

The rise of Teddy Roosevelt marked a turning point in American history—a shift from anti-imperialist leadership toward collaboration with empire. His political clique in London and Boston pushed the United States into war with Spain, seeking the conquest of the Philippines and Cuba, and advocating for a world order ruled by the “English-speaking peoples.”

This group forced the 1898 Spanish-American War against the firm opposition of President McKinley. Roosevelt was then placed on McKinley’s 1900 reelection ticket as vice president—a move opposed by McKinley himself. Soon after the 1901 inauguration, McKinley was assassinated, and Roosevelt’s rise to power sealed the nation’s shift away from Lincoln’s vision and toward imperial alignment.
